title: Filtered vector search
summary: Vector search with a metadata filter (tenant, language, date, access) can lose recall or return too few results if the filter is applied after the approximate search. Where and how the filter runs decides the outcome.
useIf: Queries carry filters: tenants, document types, dates or access groups. Choose the filter strategy deliberately.
avoidIf: Every query searches the whole index with no filter. Then the index defaults are enough.

explain.md: An ANN index finds near neighbours of the query without knowing about your filter. If you ask for the top 10 and **then** drop results that fail the filter, a selective filter can leave 2 results, or none. The index did its job, the filter ran in the wrong place. Strategies differ in **when** the filter applies.

explain.caption: Filter strategies
head: Strategy
How it works
Failure mode
rows: The filter is applied during graph traversal, so only allowed vectors are candidates
Very selective filters can slow the search, and AI Search names this `preFilter` [[tr8]]
Search first, then drop non-matching results (AI Search applies it per shard, then merges)
Fewer than k results, or none, when the filter is selective
Global top k first, then filter (AI Search `strictPostFilter`, preview)
Keep scanning the index until enough matches are found (pgvector 0.8.0 and later)
More work per query, bounded by a scan limit
The index links vectors with filtering in mind (Qdrant payload indexes, ACORN research [[tr43]])
Must exist before ingest in Qdrant, otherwise rebuild
Apply the filter first, then compare with every matching vector
Slow if the subset is large
Separate namespace or partition per tenant (Pinecone namespaces [[tr39]], pgvector list partitioning)
Many tiny partitions, cross-tenant queries are harder

explain.title: Choosing by selectivity
explain.alt: If the filter matches most rows, post-filtering and pre-filtering both work. If it is selective, use pre-filtering or iterative scans. If it is very selective or tenant-sized, use exhaustive search over the subset or a partition.
explain.src:
flowchart TD
  S{"Filter selectivity"} -->|"broad"| B["Post-filter or pre-filter"]
  S -->|"selective"| P["Pre-filter or iterative scan"]
  S -->|"very selective or tenant-sized"| X["Exhaustive over subset or partition"]

explain.md: **AI Search** exposes `vectorFilterMode`: `preFilter` (filter during HNSW traversal, best recall), `postFilter` and `strictPostFilter` (preview). Indexes created after about 2023-10-15 default to `preFilter`; older indexes default to `postFilter` and must be recreated to use `preFilter` or compression. For very selective filters consider `exhaustive: true` [[tr8]]. **pgvector** applies filters after the approximate scan, so a filter matching 10% of rows with `hnsw.ef_search` of 40 returns about 4 rows on average. Iterative scans (since 0.8.0) use `hnsw.iterative_scan` as `strict_order` or `relaxed_order`, bounded by `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (default 20,000). A B-tree index suits exact search on the filter column, a partial index suits a few distinct values and list partitioning suits many values or tenant isolation [[tr12]]. **Qdrant** needs payload indexes created before ingest for filter-aware graph edges, otherwise rebuild [[tr35]].

explain.title: Expected survivors of a post-filter

vars.v: results the ANN search examines or returns
share of vectors that match the filter

explain.example: 40 candidates and a filter matching 10% leave about 4 results, fewer than a k of 10. A 1% filter leaves less than one.

explain.title: Access filters are filters too
explain.md: A security filter (group ids, tenant id) behaves like any other filter. Apply it inside the search, never by dropping results afterwards, or selective permissions give empty answers. The access design itself belongs to the RAG security chapter.

whereToUse: Multi-tenant indexes where each query is scoped to one tenant
Access-trimmed retrieval where the filter encodes the caller's groups
Metadata-scoped search: language, product, date range, document type
Hybrid pipelines where a structured predicate narrows the vector search

use: Pre-filtering when recall matters or filters are selective
Iterative scans or partitioning in engines that filter after the scan
Exhaustive search when the filtered subset is small
avoid: Filtering on fields that were not declared filterable at index time
Assuming the engine default is pre-filtering without checking index age or version
flips: Filter becomes more selective: move from post-filter to pre-filter, iterative scan or exhaustive search
Tenants are tiny and numerous: partition or use namespaces
Latency rises under very selective pre-filters: try exhaustive search over the subset

pitfalls.symptom: Filtered queries return fewer than k results, sometimes none
pitfalls.cause: The filter runs after the ANN search and removes most candidates
pitfalls.fix: Use pre-filtering or iterative scans, raise the candidate pool, or search exhaustively over the subset

pitfalls.symptom: An older AI Search index gives thin results and cannot use compression
pitfalls.cause: Indexes created before about 2023-10-15 default to `postFilter` and cannot use `preFilter` or compression
pitfalls.fix: Recreate the index and re-index the data

pitfalls.symptom: Filter performance is poor in Qdrant after loading the data
pitfalls.cause: Payload indexes were created after ingest, so the graph lacks filter-aware edges
pitfalls.fix: Create payload indexes first, or rebuild the HNSW index

pitfalls.symptom: Results from an exhaustive filtered query differ from the ANN results
pitfalls.cause: The ANN index approximates and the filter changes its reachable candidates
pitfalls.fix: Use exact search as ground truth and measure recall with filters on

scenarios.title: Thousands of tiny tenants
scenarios.situation: A SaaS product stores vectors for 5,000 tenants in one index. Each tenant holds a tiny share of vectors and queries are always scoped to one tenant. Isolation is a hard requirement.
constraints: Each tenant is a tiny share
unknowns: How large is the biggest tenant?
scenarios.question: How do you filter?

options.name: A partition or namespace per tenant, with exact search inside small ones
options.why: Isolation is structural, per-tenant sets are small enough to scan exactly and recall does not depend on a filter.
options.tradeoff: Many partitions to manage and harder cross-tenant queries.

options.name: A tenant filter applied as a pre-filter in a shared index
options.why: One index to operate and good recall.
options.tradeoff: Extremely selective filters can cost latency, and isolation relies on a filter.

options.name: Search the shared index, then drop other tenants' results
options.why: The top results are almost all from other tenants, so little or nothing survives.
options.tradeoff: Fine only when every tenant is large and similar.

flips.if: Tenant counts exceed the product's namespace or partition limits
flips.then: Group small tenants and use a pre-filter inside each group.
Use a shared index with pre-filtering.

scenarios.takeaway: Selectivity at tenant scale pushes you toward partitions.

scenarios.title: Postgres with a 30% filter
scenarios.situation: A team uses pgvector HNSW with default settings. A language filter matches about 30% of rows and queries often return fewer than the 10 rows requested. Latency is tight.
unknowns: Is the filter on a few distinct values?
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.name: Enable iterative scans with `relaxed_order` and raise `hnsw.ef_search` moderately
options.why: The scan continues until enough matches are found, which fixes the shortfall without a new index.
options.tradeoff: Results may be slightly out of distance order and queries do more work.

options.name: Create partial indexes per language value
options.why: Exact, fast filtering for a handful of values.
options.tradeoff: One index per value, and it does not scale to many values.

options.name: Keep defaults and post-filter in application code
options.why: With `ef_search` of 40, a 30% filter leaves about 12 rows on average and often fewer than 10.
options.tradeoff: Right when the filter matches nearly every row.

scenarios.takeaway: Know where your engine applies the filter, and fix it at that point.

quiz.q: In pgvector with `hnsw.ef_search` of 40, a filter matches 10% of rows and is applied after the index scan. About how many rows come back on average?
quiz.hint: Multiply the candidate count by the selectivity.
quiz.explain: 40 candidates x 0.10 = 4 rows. If you asked for k = 10 you get fewer than requested, which is why iterative scans exist.

quiz.q: Which AI Search `vectorFilterMode` can return zero results because it takes the global top k first?
quiz.explain: `strictPostFilter` (preview) takes the global top k and then filters, so it can return none. `preFilter` filters during traversal. `postFilter` filters per shard and can miss results but is not the global-top-k variant.

quiz.q: Which are real remedies for too few filtered results in pgvector?
options: Use a partial index for a few distinct filter values
Use list partitioning for many values or tenants
quiz.explain: Iterative scans, partial indexes and partitioning address filters that apply after the scan. Lowering `ef_search` reduces candidates and makes the shortfall worse.

flashcards.front: What are the AI Search `vectorFilterMode` values?
flashcards.back: `preFilter` (during HNSW traversal, best recall), `postFilter` (per shard then merged, can miss) and `strictPostFilter` (preview, global top k first, can return zero).

flashcards.front: Why do older AI Search indexes behave differently?
flashcards.back: Indexes created before about 2023-10-15 default to `postFilter` and must be recreated to use `preFilter` or compression.

flashcards.front: Why can pgvector filtering return too few rows?
flashcards.back: Filters run after an approximate scan. With `ef_search` 40 and a 10% filter you get about 4 rows. Iterative scans (0.8.0 and later) fix this.
